first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are funnel-mechanics problems, and memory_86 plus memory_31 point directly at that mechanism: shortening onboarding and cutting signup fields lifted completion, time-to-value, and first-week activation. Fixing the funnel compounds — it raises the yield of every later lever, including any pricing response — so it is the better single slot for sustainable long-term qualified revenue than a margin-eroding price match. Promotional pricing is the obvious reflex against the competitor's entry pricing, but memory_73 carries an explicit caveat: the readout pooled two cohorts after a mid-test redefinition, so its 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' may be an artifact of cohort mixing rather than a real effect. That is exactly the kind of claim worth spending an archive pull on before betting the week, and a second pull on memory_86 confirms the onboarding effect size and whether the lift was durable or a one-quarter novelty. Downstream value risk: memory_44 says enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted, demo-request flows with higher pipeline quality. Stripping signup fields to help SMB activation can remove exactly the firmographic signals used to route enterprise leads into that assisted path, so a raw activation lift could quietly degrade qualified pipeline. The experiment must therefore measure downstream qualified revenue and enterprise routing rates, not just completion and week-one activation, and preserve or reconstruct enterprise identification. I am also treating the QoQ declines as possibly caused by the competitor's arrival (traffic-mix shift) rather than by onboarding degradation; if verification shows that, the onboarding fix may under-deliver, and referral incentives (memory_57) into the established base become the fallback. Running at standard experiment scale with a holdout rather than broad rollout, given that ambiguity.
